2024 · ACL 2024 · Benchmarks & Evals

EmoBench: Evaluating the Emotional Intelligence of Large Language Models

400 hand-crafted, bilingual multiple-choice questions built to require reasoning about implied emotional causes rather than surface pattern-matching -- and a 48-person human baseline that GPT-4 still doesn't beat.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Emotional intelligence (EI) evaluation for LLMs had, before EmoBench, mostly meant recycling existing conversational-emotion datasets -- MELD, DailyDialog, GoEmotions -- as classification tasks. The authors identify two structural problems with that approach. First, these tasks reduce to emotion recognition alone: given a short scenario, predict the emotion label, sometimes with a cause extracted as a contiguous span of the same text. That is a much narrower slice of EI than psychology recognizes -- it leaves out emotion regulation and using emotional understanding to guide a decision, which the authors group under a second capability they call Emotional Application. Second, and more damaging to measurement validity, the source datasets were designed as pattern-recognition and span-extraction problems: the cause is usually stated explicitly in the text, and the emotion usually follows a frequent, learnable pattern ("lost something" → sadness). A model can score well by matching surface regularities without modeling what the person in the scenario actually believes or values.

Figure 1 makes the failure mode concrete: "my friend borrowed a shirt from me and lost it" invites the common-pattern answer (sadness or annoyance), and if the cause is stated explicitly that's also the extractable span. But swap in a single implicit detail -- the shirt was something the narrator wanted to throw away, or it was a gift from a late grandmother -- and the correct emotion flips in ways that require inferring the narrator's perceived value of the object, which is never stated outright. A benchmark built from existing corpora structurally under-samples exactly this kind of item, because such nuance is rare and expensive to author at scale in scraped dialogue.

The paper positions two contemporaneous efforts, Wang et al. (2023) and Paech's EQ-Bench (2023), as addressing a similar gap, but notes both restrict themselves to Emotional Understanding alone and are comparatively smaller in scale -- leaving Emotional Application, and a joint theory-grounded taxonomy spanning both, unaddressed.

// how it works

The method

EmoBench operationalizes EI as two capabilities synthesized from psychological theory (Salovey & Mayer 1990; Goleman 1996; Schuller & Schuller 2018; Rivers et al. 2020): Emotional Understanding (EU) -- recognizing an individual's emotion and its cause -- and Emotional Application (EA) -- using that understanding to pick the most effective action or response inside an emotional dilemma. Both are posed as multiple-choice questions (MCQs), evaluated in both English and Chinese.

Emotional Understanding

EU scenarios are annotated against four categories: complex emotions (emotion transitions, mixtures of emotions, unexpected outcomes), personal beliefs and experiences (cultural values, sentimental value, persona/phobias), emotional cues (implicit vocal and visual cues), and perspective-taking -- borrowed directly from the theory-of-mind literature's affective false-belief (Sally-Anne-style), faux pas, and strange-story paradigms. Each scenario involves one to three individuals; for each targeted individual the model must answer two linked questions -- what emotion they feel, then why. Emotion labels are drawn from a taxonomy built on Plutchik's wheel of emotion (8 basic emotions at varying intensities, plus mixtures), merged with labels pooled from Ekman (1984), DailyDialog (Li et al., 2017), EmpatheticDialogues (Rashkin et al., 2018), and GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020). In total the authors hand-wrote 121 scenarios, producing 200 EU MCQs.

Emotional Application

EA scenarios cross two relationships (personal: friends/family/partners; social: boss/teacher/coworkers) with whose problem it is (the responder's own, or someone else's), giving four relationship-problem categories, each with 50 items for 200 EA MCQs total. Each item asks the model to choose the most effective action ("what to do?") or response ("what to say?") to an emotional dilemma. To pick a defensible gold answer for what is otherwise a subjective judgment, four annotators independently distributed a preference budget across the choices in quarter-units:

Σ Pi = 1,   Pi ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00} // each of 4 annotators splits one point of preference across the choices; scores are averaged across annotators to fix the gold answer (Fleiss' κ = 0.852)

Data construction and evaluation protocol

Scenarios were not scraped or fully LLM-generated: the authors first prompted GPT-4 for example scenarios per taxonomy category, but found its output too explicit and pattern-following to serve as final data, so GPT-4's output was used only as creative inspiration while the paper's own co-authors ("workers") hand-wrote, cross-translated (EN↔ZH), and reviewed every final item. At evaluation time, each of 12 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, ChatGLM3-6B/66B, Baichuan2-7B/13B/53B, Llama 2-7B/13B, Qwen-7B/14B, Yi-6B) is tested zero-shot in a Base setting and a chain-of-thought (CoT) setting; each MCQ is run 5 times with majority voting, and that whole procedure is repeated across 4 random permutations of the choice ordering (to control for LLMs' known choice-order bias, per Zheng et al. 2023), with the reported accuracy averaged over the 4 permutation runs. Random-choice and Majority-class baselines are included for reference.

// what they found

The results

GPT-4 leads every other tested LLM on both tasks by a wide margin. On Emotional Understanding overall accuracy (Base setting), GPT-4 scores 59.75% (English) / 54.12% (Chinese) -- both marked as the best result in the paper's Table 1 -- against the next-best model, ChatGLM3-66B, at 36.12%/35.38%, and against Random (2.62%) and Majority-class (11.5%) floors. On Emotional Application, GPT-4 again leads, reaching its best overall scores under CoT in English (75.88%) and under Base prompting in Chinese (73.75%), versus ChatGLM3-66B's best settings of 65.50% EN (Base) / 60.12% ZH (CoT) and a much higher Majority-class floor of 37.0% (many EA dilemmas have a skewed distribution of "obviously wrong" distractors, so guessing the modal answer already clears a third of items).

Chain-of-thought prompting is not a reliable win: the paper reports it "generally had little to no improvements, even hindering the performance for smaller models (particularly <14B)." The effect is visible directly in Table 1 -- Llama2-Chat-7B's EU overall accuracy falls from 11.75%/8.25% (Base) to 6.38%/6.50% (CoT), dropping below the 11.5% Majority-class floor entirely. Larger and closed-source models are comparatively CoT-stable: GPT-4's EU overall score is nearly flat between Base (59.75/54.12) and CoT (58.25/51.75).

Across EU sub-categories, perspective-taking is the weakest or joint-weakest category for most models -- it is the lowest-scoring of the four categories in both English and Chinese under every setting for GPT-4 and both Qwen models (e.g. GPT-4 Base scores 50.37% EN / 43.28% ZH on perspective-taking vs. 70.54%/75.89% on emotional cues) -- consistent, the authors note, with independent findings that LLMs struggle with theory-of-mind-style reasoning (Ullman, 2023). Personal beliefs & experiences runs a close second and is the harder category instead for several models specifically in Chinese (e.g. ChatGLM3-66B, GPT-3.5), while for Llama2-Chat-7B under CoT prompting it is emotional cues that scores lowest of all four.

To calibrate against people, the authors recruited 70 candidates, screened out anyone under 21 or unable to answer a 6-question screening quiz perfectly (48 admitted, a 31.43% rejection rate), and split them evenly across the four language×task pairs (n=12 each). Each participant answered 30 MCQs not used in screening. Human participants outperformed every LLM on both tasks; GPT-4 came the closest of any model to average human performance, particularly on Emotional Application, but "still fell short of surpassing individuals with higher emotional intelligence" -- no tested LLM beat the top-scoring humans on either task.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

EmoBench's core design idea -- author scenarios so the surface pattern and the correct answer diverge, forcing inference over an implied value or belief -- is a genuinely useful corrective to span-extraction emotion datasets, and pairing it with a real human baseline (rather than just a leaderboard of models) is rarer than it should be in this space. But a few things temper how much weight any single number here should carry.

baselines

12 LLMs from 6B to 66B -- eight open-weight models topping out at 14B (Llama 2, Baichuan2, Qwen, ChatGLM3-6B, Yi) plus four API-only models (ChatGLM3-66B, Baichuan2-53B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) -- is a reasonably broad sweep, but 8 of the 12 (Yi, both ChatGLM3 variants, all three Baichuan2 variants, both Qwen variants) are Chinese-developed, leaving only Llama 2 (2 variants) and OpenAI's two models as the non-Chinese comparison set -- no Claude or Gemini, both publicly available by the paper's February 2024 posting date. The authors themselves concede in the Limitations section that "we cannot claim our prompts were optimal, and thus, the experimental results are not indicative of LLMs' peak performance in EI."

contamination

The paper's own Limitations note that although "we did not directly include samples from GPT-4, we leveraged its generated examples to inspire our MCQs, which might have introduced a bias in our benchmark" -- a plausible circularity risk for GPT-4's own leaderboard position. Separately, all 400 questions and gold labels have been public on GitHub since the initial February 2024 preprint, so any model trained afterward on web-scraped code/data risks direct exposure to this exact benchmark; the paper reports no contamination check (e.g. n-gram overlap against pretraining corpora) for future reuse.

what's missed

Checking the published tables directly: Table 2's Baichuan2-Chat-53B row (both Base and CoT, page 8) is numerically identical, cell for cell to two decimal places, to that model's row in Table 1 (page 7) -- e.g. Base overall 34.88/34.00 appears verbatim in both an Emotional Understanding table and a structurally different Emotional Application table. Ten matched cells across two independently-scored, differently-formatted tasks is not plausible as a real result; it reads as an unflagged copy-paste error carried through to the arXiv v3 revision (17 Jul 2024, after the May 2024 ACL date), which leaves that one leaderboard row unverifiable as printed. Separately, the qualitative error analysis (Section 7, Table 3) offers three EU examples and one EA example with no aggregate statistic on how often each failure mode (misassumption, pattern reliance, topic drift, refusal) actually occurs across the full test set.

would raise confidence

A corrected Baichuan2-53B row in Table 2; a quantified breakdown of CoT failure modes rather than four illustrative examples; at least one non-Chinese, non-OpenAI frontier model in the baseline set; and a stated contamination-detection or refresh plan given the benchmark's answers have been public for well over a year.

// bottom line

The headline finding -- that even GPT-4 falls short of average, let alone top, human EI performance on carefully de-patterned scenarios -- is well-supported and is the paper's real contribution. Treat the fine-grained model-vs-model rankings below GPT-4 more cautiously: one full row of the Emotional Application table is a demonstrable duplication error, the baseline set is skewed toward Chinese open-source models with no Western closed-source competitor to GPT-4/3.5, and the construction pipeline's reliance on GPT-4-inspired scenario seeds is an acknowledged, unquantified bias risk.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. EmoBench replaces the "recognize the stated emotion" task of prior EI benchmarks with scenarios engineered so the surface pattern and the correct answer diverge -- getting the right answer requires inferring an unstated value or belief (a lost shirt's sentimental worth, a culture's punctuality norms), not extracting a labeled span.
  2. It splits machine EI into two hand-authored, bilingual (EN/ZH) MCQ tasks -- Emotional Understanding (200 items, testing emotion + cause recognition across complex emotions, personal beliefs, emotional cues, and ToM-style perspective-taking) and Emotional Application (200 items, testing choice of the most effective action/response to an emotional dilemma) -- with EA gold labels fixed by averaging four annotators' preference scores (Fleiss' κ = 0.852).
  3. Across 12 tested LLMs, GPT-4 leads on both tasks (59.75%/54.12% EU, up to 75.88%/73.75% EA) but still trails the average of 48 recruited human participants and never beats the top human scorers; chain-of-thought prompting mostly doesn't help and actively hurts sub-14B models, sometimes pushing them below the trivial majority-class baseline.
